title: The Same Model on a Vast Scale: Law’s Debt-for-Equity Swap, and the Peg That Broke It
participants: The French Crown and the Regency

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim was the conversion itself. Bondholders "traded their bonds for shares in a company whose assets were a government annuity (replacing the bonds) and a (hopefully profitable) banking license", and in summer 1719 the company proposed "to refinance the whole national debt at a favorable interest rate", financed "by issuing large amounts of equity" — again "an exchange of debt owed by the State for equity in a private company", now with tax revenues among the assets.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was the merger of monetary and fiscal machinery into one private balance sheet. The Indies Company held "a monopoly on most overseas trade, as well as other activities such as running the mints and the tobacco monopoly", then "acquired most of the contracts for tax col[lection]"; the bank, nationalised in 1718 but still headed by Law, issued the notes. The state’s revenues, its debt and its currency ended up inside the same structure.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The price of the shares became the instrument of policy rather than a signal. "The debt conversion relied on bondholders’ willingness to trade in their bonds for shares, and since they were given lengthy installments to do so, it became necessary to maintain the price of shares at a high level to entice them. Ultimately, Law was led to peg the price of shares at too high a level; and the bank found itself buying large quantities of shares, resulting in excessive money creation."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was meant to be the state’s: "If successful, it would solve France’s financial problems permanently." Instead the attempt to hold the peg required ever more note issue, and the attempts to unwind it — legal-tender decrees, forced conversion of gold and silver into notes, a May 1720 devaluation of shares and notes — produced "a run on the bank and a suspension of payments".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment was a restructuring and the scale is the point. The operations "left the bank and the company bankrupt, and Law was forced to leave the country in December 1720." By January 1721 there were "two kinds of debt outstanding: the debt owed by the king, about 1.2 billion livres ... and the debt owed by the company and the bank, about 1 billion livres", together "roughly 50 percent of France’s gross" domestic product — which is what the 1721 restructuring had to deal with.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Debt securitisation as practised across the Channel: as the article states, "the same model of debt securitization employed in the case of the Bank of England or the English South Sea Company (founded in 1711), but on a vast scale."
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The 1721 French sovereign debt restructuring, and a lasting French aversion to note-issuing banks — the negative lesson drawn from an experiment that had been explicitly modelled on the English one.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Bonds became shares; the shares had to stay high for the conversion to continue; keeping them high required the bank to buy them; buying them required issuing notes; the notes devalued the currency the shares were priced in.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That John Law was a charlatan gambler who invented paper money out of nothing to swindle France, and that the Mississippi Bubble was a confidence trick with no connection to how real states finance themselves.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The scheme was not sui generis and the source says so plainly: it was "the same model of debt securitization employed in the case of the Bank of England or the English South Sea Company (founded in 1711), but on a vast scale." The bank was chartered as "the first of its kind in France, and similar in many respects to the Bank of England", and the aims stated — to "stabilize prices, lower interest rates, and stimulate the economy" — are recognisable central-banking objectives. The diagnosis offered is a specific design error rather than fraud: "The critical mistake made by Law was to link the two instruments", which forced him to peg the share price too high and the bank to print to defend it. That is a harsher verdict in one way and a fairer one in another: it means the failure is repeatable by honest people, which a swindle would not be.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A note-issuing bank chartered in France on the Bank of England model, whose initial shareholders were holders of State bills issued in 1716 to consolidate unsecured war debts. A parallel company funded with government bonds, holding the colony of Louisiana, which grew by merger and equity issue into the Indies Company of 1719 with a monopoly on most overseas trade, the mints, the tobacco monopoly and most tax-collection contracts. A summer 1719 proposal to refinance the entire national debt, funded by large equity issues — the same debt-securitisation model as the Bank of England and the South Sea Company, on a vastly larger scale. A share price pegged too high to keep the conversion going, a bank buying shares and creating money to hold it, legal-tender decrees and forced conversion of specie, a May 1720 devaluation of shares and notes, a run and a suspension of payments. Bank and company bankrupt; Law out of the country in December 1720; and, in January 1721, about 1.2 billion livres owed by the king and about 1 billion by the company and bank, together roughly half of French output.

SOURCE CHARACTER: a signed economist's article in a Reserve Bank research publication — secondary scholarship, not a primary record, tiered and attributed as such. ON WHAT LAW’S SYSTEM ACTUALLY WAS, which is the part the popular account flattens: "Part of John Law’s plan was to replace the existing monetary system based on gold and silver coin with a paper standard, which he thought could be used to stabilize prices, lower interest rates, and stimulate the economy. To achieve this goal, he received a charter for a note-issuing bank, the first of its kind in France, and similar in many respects to the Bank of England, founded in 1694." The bank’s "initial shareholders were holders of the State bills issued in 1716 to consolidate the unsecured war debts. In effect, the bondholders traded their bonds for shares in a company whose assets were a government annuity (replacing the bonds) and a (hopefully profitable) banking license." The company grew "by a series of mergers and acquisitions, financed by equity issues, and became in 1719 the Indies Company, with a monopoly on most overseas trade, as well as other activities such as running the mints and the tobacco monopoly", then expanded into tax collection. In summer 1719 it proposed "to refinance the whole national debt at a favorable interest rate", financed by issuing "large amounts of equity" — "once again an exchange of debt owed by the State for equity in a private company". THE EXPLICIT COMPARISON: "This was the same model of debt securitization employed in the case of the Bank of England or the English South Sea Company (founded in 1711), but on a vast scale." THE DIAGNOSIS: "The critical mistake made by Law was to link the two instruments. The debt conversion relied on bondholders’ willingness to trade in their bonds for shares, and since they were given lengthy installments to do so, it became necessary to maintain the price of shares at a high level to entice them. Ultimately, Law was led to peg the price of shares at too high a level; and the bank found itself buying large quantities of shares, resulting in excessive money creation." Law, by then finance minister, made the currency sole legal tender and required conversion of gold and silver into notes; a May 1720 devaluation of shares and notes "precipitat[ed] a run on the bank and a suspension of payments"; the subsequent operations "left the bank and the company bankrupt, and Law was forced to leave the country in December 1720." ON THE SCALE OF WHAT WAS LEFT: in January 1721 there were "two kinds of debt outstanding: the debt owed by the king, about 1.2 billion livres ... and the debt owed by the company and the bank, about 1 billion livres", together "roughly 50 percent of France’s gross" domestic product.
